title: Explain the Shared Responsibility Model, and why most cloud breaches are on the customer side (misconfiguration, over-permissioned identities).
shortTitle: Explain the Shared Responsibility Model, and why most cloud breaches are on the customer side (misconfiguration, over-permissioned identities)
keyPoints: The provider secures the cloud (data centers, hardware, hypervisor); the customer secures what they put in the cloud (data, identity, config).
The dividing line moves by service model: IaaS puts OS and above on you; PaaS/managed services shrink your scope; SaaS narrows it to access and data.
Your responsibility never drops to zero: in every model you always own your data and your identity-and-access configuration.
Most breaches are customer-side because the provider's half is hardened at scale while the customer's half is bespoke and error-prone.
The two dominant failures are misconfiguration (public buckets, default passwords) and over-permissioned identities (wildcard policies).
Defenses: infrastructure-as-code, posture scanning, least privilege, short-lived credentials, encryption by default, and guardrail policies.

s1_definition.oneliner: The provider secures the cloud; you secure what you put in it: and nearly every breach is someone leaving their own box unlocked.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Provider responsibility** – security "of" the cloud: physical data centers, hardware, hypervisor, and managed-service control plane.
- **Customer responsibility** – security "in" the cloud: data, identity and access configuration, network rules, encryption settings, OS patching, and application code.
- **Service model shift** – with IaaS you own from the guest OS up; with PaaS the provider takes over OS and runtime; with SaaS your scope narrows to access and data.
- **Never zero** – in every model you always own your data and your identity configuration.
- **Breach pattern** – most cloud security failures are customer misconfiguration and over-permissioned identities, not provider failures.
s1_definition.analogy: The cloud provider is the bank building that rents you a safe-deposit box. The bank secures the vault door, walls, guards, and alarm system. But you are given the key to your own box, and you decide whether to lock it and who you hand copies to. If National Bank of India leaves a box wide open and money is stolen, that is not the vault builder's fault.

 Where Breaches Happen
 ======================

 Provider side (rare):
   Hardened by thousands of engineers, audited, standardized

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Shared Responsibility Model splits duties between the cloud provider and the customer. The provider secures the cloud: physical data centers, hardware, hypervisor, and managed-service control plane. The customer secures what they put in the cloud: data, identity and access configuration, network rules, encryption, and application code. The dividing line moves by service model, but your responsibility never reaches zero.

Most breaches land on the customer side because the provider's half is hardened at massive scale while the customer's half is bespoke. The two dominant failures are misconfiguration (public buckets, default passwords, logging off) and over-permissioned identities (wildcard policies that grant all actions on all resources). The defenses are infrastructure-as-code, posture scanning, least privilege, short-lived credentials, encryption by default, and guardrail policies.

At National Bank of India I put all configuration into infrastructure-as-code so settings are reviewed and version-controlled, ran continuous posture scanning to catch public buckets and open ports, and enforced least privilege with short-lived temporary credentials instead of static keys.

Remember one sentence: the provider secures the cloud infrastructure, but you always own your data, your identity configuration, and the misconfigurations that cause most breaches.
